rationale: Firing a gun at a person to wound shows intent to cause serious bodily harm/depraved heart; transferred intent makes the killing murder. No claims to assess; no other option competes.
evidence: Common-law murder: malice includes intent to inflict grievous bodily harm; transferred intent doctrine (LaFave, Criminal Law).

rationale: Externalist (supernaturalist) theories of life's meaning are mostly framed from a religious (God-centered) standpoint. 'Spiritual' is a weaker near-synonym, but 'religious' is the standard term; no material defect.
evidence: Metz, 'The Meaning of Life', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: supernaturalism, God-centered views.

rationale: Arriving on time for work is cultural, but so are following a dress code (B) and food preferences (E); B is at least as clearly culturally based as C. Nothing makes C uniquely best.
evidence: Conceptual: dress codes and punctuality norms both vary by culture (cross-cultural psychology texts).

rationale: I accept the reviewers' claim for G. The lease ran from 1985 to 1992, and a tenant's possession during the term is not hostile, so the 20-year period could not have run by 2009. The key A (tenant believed the lease continued, so possession was permissive) is also defensible. Both explain why the organization prevails.
evidence: Adverse possession requires hostile possession; a tenant holding under a lease is permissive until the term ends or title is repudiated (Restatement/property hornbooks). 1992+20=2012>2009.

rationale: Warlordism, strongmen and coups are internal threats arising from weak state institutions. A refugee influx comes from outside, so it is the odd one out.
evidence: Collins (ed.), Contemporary Security Studies, ch. on weak states: internal threats (warlords, strongmen, coups).

rationale: I (a colleague's number for emergency calls) is the standard EPPP answer. J (a colleague provides emergency sessions only while regular appointments pause) gives essentially the same coverage. G (tell clients ahead) is also good practice. The line between I and J is thin.
evidence: APA Ethics Code 3.12 Interruption of Psychological Services (make reasonable efforts to plan for continuity of care).

rationale: Partial performance does not end a contract. Fulfillment (G) and expiration of the term (C) also end it, but by performance or by the contract's own terms, not by operation of law. On a strict reading, C and G also 'will not terminate by operation of law'. On a looser reading only D fits.
evidence: Contract-law hornbooks classify discharge as by performance, agreement, operation of law (death, bankruptcy, impossibility, illegality) or breach.

rationale: The southern prairie provinces are linked with Ukrainian and other Eastern European settlers, not African Americans, so B is clearly wrong. Florida–Native Americans (Seminole) and New England–Latin Americans are weaker associations but defensible, so B is the best answer.
evidence: Human geography texts on North American ethnic regions (prairie provinces: Ukrainian/Eastern European settlement).

rationale: ReLU's gradient is 0 for x<0, and σ'(x)=σ(1-σ)≤1/4, so Statement 1 is true. Sigmoid's derivative is continuous and ReLU's derivative jumps at 0, so Statement 2 is true. True, True.
evidence: Calculation: max σ(1-σ)=0.25 at σ=0.5; ReLU' is a step function.

rationale: There is no attempted sale because the defendant knew it was oregano, and no solicitation because he did not intend the crime to happen. False pretenses (B) fits. Theft by deception (H) is the MPC/modern name for the same offense, so an expert would accept H too.
evidence: Model Penal Code §223.3 Theft by Deception (consolidates false pretenses); LaFave on false pretenses.

rationale: Fats and oils are about 95% or more triacylglycerols. Option B '95-100%' is effectively the same range as the key A '>95%', so the option set has two equivalent correct answers.
evidence: Biochemistry/nutrition texts: fats and oils are >95% triacylglycerols.

rationale: Classical equipartition: a 3D oscillator has 6 quadratic terms × kT/2 = 3kT.
evidence: Equipartition theorem calculation.

rationale: Paying rent acknowledged the owner's title, which broke hostility. The period restarted in 2002, so it had not run by 2011 (19 years even if the two periods could be tacked). The key I gives the reason. A ('statutory period not met at filing') is also correct, and an expert would accept it.
evidence: Adverse possession: acknowledgment of the owner's title (paying rent) breaks continuity/hostility. Calculation: 1990-2000 plus 2002-2011 is 19 years, under 20.

rationale: I accept the reviewers' claim for D. The standard definition of senescence is biological aging. The key I ('increased vulnerability') matches some gerontology texts' gloss, so both are defensible; D is arguably the better answer.
evidence: Wikipedia 'Senescence': 'Senescence or biological aging is the gradual deterioration of functional characteristics'; Merriam-Webster.

rationale: In an unfavourable mandibular body fracture, the anterior fragment is pulled down by the digastric (I). The posterior fragment is also pulled up by masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid (F), and medially by the medial pterygoid in vertically unfavourable fractures (J). Several options are correct.
evidence: Oral and maxillofacial surgery texts (e.g. Fonseca): muscle pull on fragments in favourable vs unfavourable mandible fractures.

rationale: I accept the reviewers' claim for A. Cooper v. Oklahoma (1996) struck down requiring a defendant to prove incompetence by clear and convincing evidence. Medina v. California allows a state to put the burden on the defendant by a preponderance. The key D wrongly says the prosecution must prove competency.
evidence: Cooper v. Oklahoma, 517 U.S. 348 (1996); Medina v. California, 505 U.S. 437 (1992).

rationale: Dun & Bradstreet is the classic source of business credit ratings for retailers. Equifax is mainly a consumer credit bureau.
evidence: Dun & Bradstreet business credit reports (D&B Rating).

rationale: I accept the reviewers' claim for B. Current consensus puts human arrival in Australia at about 50,000 years ago or earlier (some say 65,000, Madjedbebe). 'Soon after 40,000' reflects older estimates, so the key is stale.
evidence: Wikipedia 'Archaeology of Australia'; O'Connell & Allen 2004/2015 (~47-50 ka); Clarkson et al. 2017 (65 ka).

rationale: A preliminary consultation with a prospective client is privileged. A parent present for a minor does not destroy confidentiality, and suing does not waive privilege over the communications. D is also true but is a weaker reason, so C is best.
evidence: FRE 501 / common-law attorney-client privilege; Restatement (Third) Law Governing Lawyers §§70, 15 (prospective clients).

rationale: In GDP = C+I+G+X, X is net exports (exports minus imports).
evidence: Standard macroeconomics national income identity.

evidence: Conceptual: social-scale hierarchy vs institutions (sociology/global studies texts).

evidence: Fagan, People of the Earth; Sungir' burials (Wikipedia 'Sungir').

rationale: The key H says the student's character is 'directly at issue', but the student's honesty is not an element of malicious prosecution. Using it to show he lied in the complaint is propensity use, barred by FRE 404(a). No option states the law cleanly.
evidence: FRE 404(a), 405(b); elements of malicious prosecution (Restatement (Second) Torts §653).

rationale: Under United States v. Lovasco (1977), investigative delay does not violate due process even when it causes some prejudice, so the motion is denied and the key E fits. H (the prosecutor had a valid reason) and A (no infringement of rights) say nearly the same thing.
evidence: United States v. Lovasco, 431 U.S. 783 (1977); United States v. Marion, 404 U.S. 307 (1971).

rationale: Male-to-male transmission rules out X-linked inheritance and is typical of autosomal dominant inheritance (key I). It is also the defining feature of Y-linked inheritance (G), which is passed only father to son. Two options are correct.
evidence: Medical genetics texts (e.g. Thompson & Thompson): Y-linked traits pass exclusively father to son.

evidence: Calculation: X_eq = 0.16/4 = 0.04 pu; SCL = 20/0.04 = 500 MVA.

rationale: A loathsome disease in print is libel per se, so no special damages are needed (key C). Under Gertz, a private-figure plaintiff needs only negligence, so F ('negligently... enough to sustain a libel claim') is also correct and J is defensible.
evidence: Gertz v. Robert Welch, 418 U.S. 323 (1974); Restatement (Second) Torts §§569, 572.

evidence: Indianapolis Motor Speedway / Indianapolis 500 history.
